Eighteen months ago, it set up an AI center of excellence (CoE) of 12 people with a shared platform, security standards and reusable components. The CoE charges each brand the full cost of every project it delivers, including a share of the platform's running costs. Brand leaders rate the CoE's work highly on the projects they have used it for. Three brands now hire contractors to build AI tools outside the CoE, citing its prices, and those tools do not follow the CoE's security standards. As brands have left, the CoE has twice raised its project price to cover the platform's fixed costs. Attendance at the CoE's monthly community call has fallen by half.

What should the group change?

options.text: Require every brand to build AI tools through the CoE, and move the tools built by contractors onto the shared platform within six months.
Fund the shared platform and standards from the group budget, and charge brands only for the build work on their own projects.
Cut the CoE to six people to lower its project price, and keep charging each brand the full cost of the work that it requests.
Publish the CoE's security standards for contractors to follow, and turn the monthly call into a quarterly showcase of brand projects.

questions.explanation:
A: A mandate would bring the contractor tools under the CoE's standards, which addresses a real risk. But it forces brands to pay prices they have already rejected, and those prices keep rising because the platform's fixed cost is spread over fewer projects. Brands that are forced to use a service they see as overpriced tend to resist it.

B: A CoE helps scaling when units can afford to build on its shared foundations. Charging the platform's fixed costs to each project means every brand that leaves raises the price for the rest, which pushes more brands to contractors and outside the security standards. Funding the platform and standards centrally treats them as shared assets that every brand benefits from, while brands still pay for work done for them. AWS CAF for AI advises aligning a CoE's incentives with the business and recognizing the cost of maintaining disparate systems.

C: A smaller team would cut people costs. But the platform's fixed costs remain and are still charged to projects, so the price pressure continues, and the CoE would have half the capacity for the brands that still use it. Brand leaders already rate its work highly; the problem is how it is paid for, not its size.

D: Sharing standards with contractors could reduce some security risk, and a showcase might revive interest. But brands would keep building separately on separate tools, losing the reuse the CoE was set up to provide, while the pricing that drives them away stays unchanged.

questions.text:
A wind farm operator runs 600 turbines. Its data science team built a machine learning (ML) model that gives each turbine a percentage chance of a gearbox fault within 60 days, so that planners can schedule inspections before faults occur. After a year, planners have inspected fewer than one in five of the turbines that the model scored above 50 percent. A review found:

- Across the year, turbines scored around 70 percent had gearbox faults about 70 percent of the time.
- Planners say the model is unreliable, and several pointed to turbines scored at 70 percent that kept running without a fault.
- Scores appear in a separate web portal, and planners schedule crews from a spreadsheet.
- Planners have not been told which sensor readings drive each turbine's score.

Which gap MOST likely explains why planners act on so few of the scores?

options.text: Planners cannot see which sensor readings drive each score, so they have no way to judge whether a particular score deserves an inspection.
The scores sit in a portal apart from the spreadsheet that planners schedule from, so acting on them means copying them across by hand.
The model needs more fault history, since turbines scored at 70 percent that ran without faults show it is often wrong about single turbines.
Planners treat each score as a firm yes-or-no forecast, so a likely fault that does not happen looks to them like the model getting it wrong.

questions.explanation:
A: Explanations of which readings drive a score can build trust, but the planners' objection is not that scores are puzzling. They call the model unreliable because some high-scoring turbines did not fail. Knowing the sensor drivers would not change how they read a 70 percent chance, so this people gap is real but not the one blocking action.

B: Copying scores between systems adds effort, and fixing it would help. But planners give a reason for not acting, unreliability, and that reason would remain if the scores appeared in their spreadsheet. A technology fix for a skills gap leaves the scores just as ignored.

C: A 70 percent score means that about three in ten such turbines are expected to run without a fault. The year's results match the scores closely, so the model is well calibrated. Turbines that did not fail are what the scores predicted, not evidence of error, and more history would not change that.

D: The model is doing what it should: turbines scored around 70 percent failed about 70 percent of the time. Planners nevertheless count every high score without a fault as a mistake, which means they read a probability as a promise. That is a people capability gap in understanding probabilistic output, and until it is closed, accurate scores will keep being dismissed.

questions.text:
A property letting agency manages 14,000 rented homes for private landlords. Its three-year strategy makes round-the-clock answers to tenants' and landlords' questions the main way it will win landlords from rivals. Staff have used a licensed generative AI (GenAI) assistant for a year to draft emails, and they edit about a third of its drafts before sending. No AI system talks directly to customers.

A rival agency launched a customer chat assistant six months ago and advertises it to landlords. Answers about deposits, repairs and notice periods must follow tenancy law, and a wrong answer can expose the agency to claims. Ten years of tenant emails and staff replies are stored in the agency's archive, and the legal team has offered to review a list of standard answers.

This year's budget funds one development investment. Which investment should the agency make?

options.text: Launch a customer chat assistant this year after testing it on 500 archived tenant questions, with a handover to staff when it cannot answer.
Build the assistant first for staff to use when answering tenants, and track where they correct its answers before opening it to customers.
Fine-tune a model on the archived emails and replies, check its answers against the staff replies, and launch it to customers this year.
Have the legal team approve standard answers to the 200 most common questions this year, and build a customer assistant from them next year.

questions.explanation:
A: A pre-launch test on archived questions is useful, but it moves the agency straight from internal drafting to unsupervised answers about tenancy law. Staff still change a third of the current assistant's drafts, and a handover helps only when the assistant knows it cannot answer; a confident wrong answer about a deposit reaches the tenant. Past questions also cannot show how the assistant handles the questions customers will actually ask.

B: Progression should start from current maturity: AI is used only internally, and its drafts still need frequent human edits. An assistant that staff use to answer tenants delivers value this year, keeps a person between the AI and the customer while answers involve tenancy law, and shows from live use where and how often answers go wrong. That evidence is what the agency needs to decide when, and for which questions, the assistant can safely face customers.

C: Fine-tuning teaches the model to sound like the agency's past replies, and checking against those replies measures resemblance, not legal correctness. Ten years of replies include advice given under earlier rules and mistakes. The agency would launch customer-facing AI with a test that rewards copying its archive.

D: Legally approved answers reduce risk, but spending the year's one investment on a fixed answer list delays any AI capability by a year while the rival's assistant is already advertised. A list of 200 answers also builds no experience of running an AI assistant or judging its output, which is the capability the strategy depends on.

questions.text:
A lift and escalator maintenance company employs 900 field technicians. It is piloting a generative AI assistant that answers technicians' questions by retrieving passages from the company's service documents. A review of the pilot found:

- The assistant draws on 40,000 files across three shared drives. About a quarter are scanned pages that it cannot read.
- On 500 test questions, 81 percent of answers were correct. Most wrong answers quoted, word for word, a procedure found in the files.
- Manufacturers' service bulletins that change a procedure are filed in a separate folder from the manuals they amend.
- Many manuals were saved again after each revision under similar file names.
- Technicians in two regions keep their own repair notes on a team wiki.

What should the company do FIRST to improve the assistant's answers?

options.text: Convert the scanned pages to searchable text and add them to the files that the assistant searches when it answers technicians.
Add the two regions' repair notes from the team wiki to the documents that the assistant searches when it answers technicians.
Identify the current revision of each manual and the bulletins that amend it, and remove superseded copies from what the assistant searches.
Fine-tune the model on the manuals and bulletins, and have it answer from what it has learned instead of searching the files.

questions.explanation:
A: Unreadable scans leave gaps, which tend to produce missing or partial answers. The wrong answers here quoted text the assistant did find, so adding more files would not correct them, and it would add any outdated scanned revisions to the mix.

B: Field notes may add useful knowledge, but they are another uncontrolled source, and the wrong answers did not come from missing knowledge. Adding them before the existing documents are sorted out gives the assistant more text whose currency nobody has checked.

C: A retrieval-based assistant is only as good as the documents it retrieves. Wrong answers that quote the files word for word mean the assistant found real text, but often the wrong version: manuals saved again after each revision under similar names, and bulletins that change procedures stored apart from the manuals. Establishing which content is current and removing superseded copies fixes the data-quality problem behind the errors.

D: Fine-tuning on the same mixed set of old and new revisions would teach the model the conflicting procedures, and a fine-tuned model cannot show which document an answer came from. It also needs retraining whenever a bulletin changes a procedure, while retrieval picks up current documents once they are indexed.

questions.text:
A medical device manufacturer wants a generative AI assistant that answers its 2,500 staff's questions from its 15,000 standard operating procedures (SOPs). The SOPs use the company's own part codes and terms, and about 200 of them are revised each month. Use is expected to grow as more sites join during the first year, though nobody can yet say by how much. The company runs its business applications on AWS. The IT director proposes buying eight GPU servers for the company's data center to host an open-weight model, because SOP content is confidential and must not be used to train any provider's models. The security lead agrees with that concern and asks that SOP content be processed only on capacity reserved for the company.

Which approach should the company take?

options.text: Call a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock on demand, paying for the tokens used, and answer each question from retrieved SOP passages.
Buy the GPU servers to host an open-weight model in the company's data center, and answer each question from retrieved SOP passages.
Reserve Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock for the company's own use, and answer each question from retrieved SOP passages.
Fine-tune a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock on all 15,000 SOPs so that it learns the company's terms, and answer from the tuned model.

questions.explanation:
A: Amazon Bedrock does not use customers' prompts or outputs to train models and does not share them with model providers, so the confidentiality concern is met without owning or reserving capacity. On-demand pricing charges for the tokens processed, which suits a workload whose growth is still unknown, and there is no hardware to run. Retrieving SOP passages for each question supplies the company's own terms and picks up revised SOPs once they are indexed.

B: Owned servers keep data in-house, but so does a managed service that does not train on customer data, so the hardware buys no extra confidentiality. The company would size eight servers before it knows how use will grow, pay up front, and take on running GPU hardware outside the AWS environment where its applications already run.

C: Provisioned Throughput buys dedicated model capacity for higher, consistent throughput at a committed rate; it is a capacity and cost choice, not a data-protection control. On-demand requests are not used for training either. Committing to reserved capacity before usage is known risks paying for capacity that sits idle.

D: Fine-tuning can teach terminology, but it takes hours to days and would need repeating as about 200 SOPs change each month, so answers would lag behind current procedures. A fine-tuned model also cannot point to the SOP an answer came from, and it can mix up procedures. Retrieval is the recommended starting point for answering questions from a company's own documents.

questions.text:
A mortgage lender will give its 180 underwriters an AI tool that gathers documents and drafts the first assessment of each application. Leaders expect files to take about 40 percent less time once the tool is in full use, and they have confirmed that no underwriting roles will be cut. The rollout starts in two months, team by team.

In a three-month pilot, 12 underwriters completed about 15 percent fewer files than usual in the first five weeks, then overtook their old pace. Underwriters earn a monthly bonus based on the number of files they complete. Most underwriters outside the pilot have heard about it only through informal conversations, and the pilot underwriters are keen to describe how the tool has changed their work.

What should the communication plan emphasize?

options.text: The pilot's time saving per file, with pilot underwriters showing colleagues at team meetings how they now work with the tool.
Leaders' commitment that no underwriting roles will be cut, repeated by the head of underwriting at each stage of the rollout.
Each team's training and go-live dates, with a named contact in every team who can answer questions as the rollout proceeds.
The slower output to expect in the first weeks of use, and when and how bonus targets will be adjusted during that period.

questions.explanation:
A: Peer stories are a strong way to build interest, but leading with the end-state saving sets the expectation that work speeds up at once. When output then falls for several weeks and bonuses shrink, staff will see the gap between the message and their experience, and trust in the change drops just as it matters most.

B: Job security is a common concern, and repeating the commitment does no harm, but it is already settled. The effect underwriters will feel first is on their pay, which the pilot shows will dip before it improves. A message that answers a question already answered leaves the one that will affect them unaddressed.

C: Clear dates and a named contact help a phased rollout run smoothly, and they address timing. They say nothing about what results to expect or how pay will be treated while people learn the tool, which is where this rollout will hurt first.

D: Communication about AI should set realistic outcome expectations, including how performance changes during adoption, and explain the effect on people's own work and pay. The pilot shows a learning dip of about 15 percent before gains appear, and pay is tied to files completed. Saying in advance that the dip is expected, and how targets will treat it, prevents a normal learning curve from being read as failure or as a pay cut.

questions.text:
An aerospace parts manufacturer with 3,500 employees wants staff in every function to apply AI to their own work within two years. Last year, 80 percent of staff completed a two-hour online course on generative AI basics, and course ratings were high. The transformation lead reports:

- An ideas portal has collected 240 AI ideas from staff. The AI team reviewed 30 of them and found that most relied on data the company does not hold or repeated what existing software already does.
- Engineers have asked for an advanced course on how models are trained and evaluated.
- A two-day hackathon last spring drew 60 staff, and the executive team enjoyed judging the demonstrations.
- The AI team of five also supports the company's two production models.

Which approach will do the MOST to build AI literacy across the company?

options.text: Offer the advanced course on model training and evaluation to all staff who finished the basics course, starting with the engineers who asked.
Fund small proof-of-concept projects in which teams test one of their own portal ideas on company data for a few weeks, then decide whether to continue.
Run a hackathon every quarter at each site, with teams building prototypes from portal ideas and the executive team judging the results.
Have the AI team publish a monthly review of portal ideas, explaining why each was or was not taken forward, for all staff to read.

questions.explanation:
A: Deeper technical content suits people who will build models, but most staff need to judge where AI fits their work, not how models are trained. Another course adds knowledge of the same kind that the basics course already gave, without the practice of testing an idea against real conditions.

B: Staff know the basics but cannot yet judge which ideas are workable: most ideas reviewed depended on missing data or duplicated existing software. A small proof of concept makes a team test its own idea on the data it would really use and then decide whether it is worth continuing. Doing that on their own work is how judgment about data, feasibility and value is learned, and the decision step ties the learning to a business outcome.

C: Hackathons generate energy and prototypes, and the last one was popular. But two days of building for a judged demonstration rewards what looks impressive, not whether the data exists or the problem is already solved. Teams rarely confront those questions before the event ends, so the judgment that is missing does not develop.

D: Explaining decisions is good feedback, but reading about other people's ideas is passive learning. Staff would learn which ideas failed without practising how to test their own, and the AI team would carry the full review load for every idea.

questions.text:
A district heating company supplies hot water to 60,000 homes from three plants. A machine learning (ML) system now adjusts the plants' temperatures and pump settings every few minutes, a task that control-room operators used to do by hand. Each shift has three operators, who now watch the system and take over when it hands back control. A review of the first year found:

- Fuel use fell 9 percent, and operators overrode the system on fewer than one shift in fifty.
- The system handed back control twice, during a sensor failure and a cold snap. Both times operators took about twice as long as in earlier years to steady the network.
- Four of the twelve operators joined after the system went live.
- Operators describe their shifts as long periods of watching screens.
- The vendor's next release will cover cold snaps.

How should the company design the operators' roles?

options.text: Operators spend regular sessions on a plant simulator practising failures and extreme conditions, while the system handles routine adjustments.
Operators approve each of the system's setting changes before it takes effect, which keeps them engaged with how the network is running.
Operators stay in their monitoring role, and the company installs the vendor's next release to reduce the events that need a handover.
Operators review the system's decisions at the end of each shift and send the vendor notes on any decisions that look wrong.

questions.explanation:
A: When an AI system handles routine work, people keep the role it cannot do: taking over in unusual conditions. That role needs the hands-on skill that routine work used to build, and here it is fading: takeovers took twice as long, and a third of the operators have never run the network by hand. Regular simulator practice of failures and extremes keeps that skill ready, so oversight works when it is needed, while the system keeps the fuel savings on routine adjustments.

B: Approving every change adds human involvement, but with changes every few minutes and overrides on fewer than one shift in fifty, approvals soon become routine sign-offs. Operators would still not practise the rare, difficult situations in which they must take over, and the delay could cost some of the fuel savings.

C: Covering cold snaps reduces one kind of handover, but no release can anticipate every sensor failure or new condition, and the system will still hand back control in situations nobody planned for. Operators who only watch will be even less practised when that happens.

D: Feedback to the vendor helps improve the system and is worth having, but reviewing routine decisions after the event does not build the skill of steadying the network in a live failure. The gap shown in the takeovers would remain.

questions.text:
A car servicing chain is extending a generative AI assistant that drafts repair estimates and plain-language explanations of faults for customers. A four-month pilot at 20 company-owned garages halved the time to send an estimate, and complaints about unclear estimates fell. The chain plans to extend the assistant to all 300 garages over six months, including 120 franchised garages trading under four local brands. A review finds:

- The assistant looks up parts and labour times in the company-owned garages' catalogue system. Franchised garages use a different catalogue system from another supplier.
- The pilot's monthly AI cost was read from the AWS bill as a single figure for the whole account.
- In the pilot, a service adviser checked each estimate before it reached the customer.
- Pilot garage managers volunteered for the pilot and promote the assistant to their staff.
- Franchise owners want customer explanations to match each brand's own tone.

Which actions should the chain take as it scales the assistant? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Remove the service adviser's check at garages where the assistant's estimates closely match final invoices during their first month of use.
Test the assistant's estimates at a few franchised garages on their own catalogue system before the other franchised garages join.
Hold each wave of garages back until every garage in it has a manager who volunteers to champion the assistant, as in the pilot.
Fine-tune a separate copy of the model for each of the four franchise brands, and use those copies at the franchised garages.
Tag the assistant's usage by garage group, and review its costs in AWS Cost Explorer as each wave of garages goes live.

questions.explanation:
A: One month of matching invoices at a new garage is a thin basis for removing the only human check, especially at franchised garages whose parts data the assistant has never used. The adviser's check is what kept errors away from customers in the pilot, and it should stay until performance is shown across the wider estate.

B: Pilot results hold only for the conditions in which they were measured. The assistant's estimates depend on parts and labour data, and the franchised garages hold that data in a different system from another supplier. Testing at a few franchised garages first shows whether estimates stay accurate on that data before 120 garages depend on it.

C: Volunteer champions can help adoption, but making every garage find one before it joins would stall the rollout on a condition many garages may never meet. Champions support adoption; they do not protect continuity or performance at scale.

D: Tone and style can be set through prompt instructions for each brand, which is the recommended first step before fine-tuning. Four fine-tuned copies would each need training data, testing and upkeep, multiplying cost and maintenance at the moment of scaling, and they do nothing about the catalogue difference.

E: Under consumption-based pricing, costs grow with use, and the chain is going from 20 garages to 300, including garages on a different data system that may use the assistant differently. A single account-wide figure cannot show which garages drive cost. Tagging usage, for example through application inference profiles in Amazon Bedrock, lets Cost Explorer group costs by garage group, so the chain can see each wave's cost against its benefit as it goes live.
